title: Can AI do covenant monitoring a private credit fund can trust?
description: Covenant monitoring with AI for private credit funds: who signs what, three builds, a test plan and our check of eight BDC filings.
verdict: AI can read borrower packages, spread the numbers and recompute covenants; an analyst still checks every flagged figure[^33][^36].
Private credit defaults hit a record in 2026, and the Fed reads heavy pay-in-kind (PIK) interest as a strain signal[^24][^21].
Our check of eight listed lenders' filings: loans on non-accrual are marked at roughly 19% to 61% of cost[^7][^5].
Filings report PIK so differently that five of eight needed our own arithmetic or a second document to compare[^1][^4].
The SEC says gaps in borrower reporting don't excuse fair value duties; your board or designee still owns each mark[^13][^11].

summary: Covenant monitoring checks each borrower's quarterly numbers against its loan terms; AI reads the package, spreads the figures, recomputes covenants and flags drift[^28][^33]. The aim is to spot trouble early[^29][^34]. What makes or breaks it: an analyst checks every flagged number, and nobody takes the borrower's own math on trust[^29][^36].
humanRole: Your people keep every decision: analysts own the numbers, portfolio heads the watchlist, and the board or valuation designee each fair value mark[^29][^33][^11].

Credit analyst: checks every number the AI flags and reconciles its covenant math with the borrower's certificate[^29][^36]. Add-backs, costs the borrower adds back to EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization), stay the analyst's call[^32].

Head of portfolio management: decides watchlist moves and what to raise with the borrower[^33]. Waivers and amendments need written consent from the Required Lenders, the lender majority the credit agreement names[^20].
Board or valuation designee: owns each fair value mark, and must test and oversee the methods behind it[^11][^12]. AI drafts the inputs and a change memo; it does not set the mark[^13].
Operations analyst: confirms each package arrived complete and on time[^28]. A late or resubmitted certificate is a signal in itself[^31].
teamAfter: Analysts watch more loans, more often. One vendor reports monitoring time per loan fell from nine hours to one, and analysts covered 12 loans each instead of 4 (vendor claim)[^50].
Analysts spend the time on early-warning work. It matters more now: covenant-lite loans, with no quarterly tests, rose from 4% to 21% of deals, 2023 to 2025[^38][^30].
Portfolio heads edit a memo draft instead of writing from a blank page, and spend the time with borrowers whose numbers drift[^33][^34].
Among US firms where AI changed tasks, 66% use it only to help staff; 2% saw AI-related employment fall[^37].

example.input: Illustrative: a $1.5B direct lender with 60 borrowers and three analysts gets third-quarter packages in November, as PDFs and Excel files[^28]. Each holds financial statements and a compliance certificate with the borrower's own covenant math[^29].
example.output: The AI maps each line to the fund's chart and recomputes debt-to-EBITDA and interest coverage from the agreement's own definitions. Flags: a ratio 0.3x off the certificate from an add-back, a second PIK quarter, and revenue down 18% despite reported headroom. The analyst checks each flag; the portfolio head moves one name to the watchlist; the valuation team cites it in the mark memo.

tables.title: Which monitoring steps can AI take, and who signs?
tables.intro: AI can take intake, spreading, covenant recompute, early-warning flags, valuation inputs and memo drafts, while analysts, portfolio heads and the board still sign[^28][^33]. Each row shows what happens today, what AI takes on and who signs.

rows.name: Intake
cells: Packages arrive by email and portal, 45 to 60 days after quarter end[^28]
Sorts and files each package; flags missing or late items
Operations analyst confirms it is complete

rows.name: Spreading
cells: An analyst keys statements into the fund's standard template, called the spread
Pulls and maps line items, with a confidence score per cell (vendor feature)[^48]
Analyst reviews every low-confidence cell[^36]

rows.name: Covenant test
cells: Read off the borrower's own certificate[^29]
Recomputes each ratio from the agreement's definitions
Analyst reconciles any gap with the borrower

rows.name: Early warning
cells: A quarterly look at each name
Flags trends: PIK, maturity extensions, revenue, liquidity, late delivery[^21][^24]
Head of portfolio management decides the watchlist

rows.name: Valuation support
cells: Discounted cash flow or yield model calibrated at origination[^23]
Drafts updated inputs and a change memo
Board or valuation designee signs the mark[^11]

rows.name: Credit memo
cells: Written from scratch each quarter
Drafts from the spread and the flags
Analyst edits and signs

recipes.name: 1. Small team: package intake and spreading with a review queue
recipes.when: Funds with a few analysts who re-key borrower PDFs into Excel each quarter[^28]. Builds 2 and 3 run on its spreads, so most funds start here.
flow: Operations analyst: set one folder and naming rule for every borrower package
Builder, in-house or hired: connect a document extraction service to that folder
Analyst: map each borrower's lines to the fund's chart of accounts, once
Analyst: run the AI fill; each cell gets a confidence score
Analyst: review every low-confidence or changed cell
Head of portfolio management: sign off the quarter's spreads
recipes.cost: Extraction lists at $10 per 1,000 pages on Azure, or $0.015 a page for Amazon Textract tables (read 26 Nov 2026)[^43][^44]. Sixty borrowers, four quarters, 80 pages each: 19,200 pages, about $192 a year at Azure's rate.

recipes.name: 2. Mid-size team: covenant recompute and headroom tracker
recipes.when: Funds whose agreements carry their own definitions, add-back caps and cure limits[^20][^28]. The borrower's certificate shows its math, not yours[^29].
flow: Credit analyst or counsel: encode each agreement's definitions, add-back caps and cure limits
Analyst: run the recompute on each quarter's spread
Analyst: reconcile every gap against the borrower's certificate
Analyst: log each equity cure used against the agreement's limit
Head of portfolio management: track headroom, the room left before each covenant breaks, and decide next steps
Required Lenders: approve any waiver or amendment in writing
recipes.cost: Model fees are small: Claude Sonnet 5.5 lists $2 per million tokens (word pieces) read and $10 written (read 26 Nov 2026)[^45]. Encoding each agreement's definitions is the real cost, in analyst and counsel time.

recipes.name: 3. Larger book: early-warning flags and a memo draft
recipes.when: Funds with many names, where covenant-lite deals leave fewer tripwires[^38]. Early signals matter most when there is no covenant to trip.
flow: Head of portfolio management: pick the signals, such as PIK toggles, maturity extensions, amendments, late delivery, revenue drop and liquidity
Builder, in-house or hired: score each name on those signals every quarter
Analyst: edit the AI's one-page memo draft for each flagged name
Head of portfolio management: decide watchlist moves
Valuation designee: use the memo as an input, never as the mark
recipes.cost: The same small extraction and model fees as builds 1 and 2[^43][^45]. No monitoring platform we checked publishes a price, so a bought version means a quote[^46][^47].

ownData.title: What do eight public BDC filings show about non-accruals and PIK?
ownData.intro: Non-accruals, loans no longer booking interest, run 1.8% to 14.2% of cost and are carried at 19% to 61% of cost[^5][^7]. PIK makes up about 4.5% to 16.4% of investment income[^6][^1]. We read the latest SEC filings of eight listed business development companies (BDCs) on 26 Nov 2026, for periods ended 30 Sep 2026[^2][^9].
rows: Not stated; our sum of $58M and $67M of $763M[^1]
10-Q gives fair value only; cost rate and PIK from the 8-K[^3][^4]
Stated as % of total investment income[^5]
8.2%, nine months, from the cash-flow statement[^7]
Not stated as %; quarterly split incomplete[^7]
10-K, fiscal year to 30 Sep 2026, filed 17 Nov 2026
8.2%, fiscal year and Q4, excluding purchase premium amortization[^10]
ownData.note: Limits: denominators, PIK definitions, periods and non-accrual policies differ by filer, and ~ marks a ratio built from rounded percentages. TCPC's PIK covers nine months and FSK's counts PIK interest only[^7][^4]. Eight large public BDCs are a sample, not your book; this shows direction, not investment advice, and ranks no BDC.

rules.name: SEC Rule 2a-5, good faith determinations of fair value
rules.what: Applies to registered funds and BDCs[^12]. The board or its valuation designee must assess valuation risks, select and test methods, oversee pricing services and report to the board[^11]. AI output feeds that process; the designee still decides.

rules.name: SEC staff statement on fair value of private assets
rules.status: Issued 28 Sep 2026 (staff view, not a rule)
rules.what: Gaps in borrower reporting don't excuse the fair value duty[^13][^14]. Staff expect calibration to the transaction price, reassessed over time[^13]. Record which borrower data was missing and how each mark handled it.

rules.name: SEC fiscal year 2027 examination priorities
rules.what: Private credit valuation is an exam focus[^15][^16]. Expect examiners to ask how each mark used the latest borrower data.

rules.name: Federal Reserve SR 26-2, model risk management
rules.what: It replaced SR 11-7 and leaves generative and agentic AI out of scope, while saying firms' own governance should still cover them[^22]. Funds aren't bound by it. It is a useful checklist for bank-affiliated lenders and for vetting vendor models.

howToTest: Run the tool on last quarter's packages for 10 borrowers in one fund, including two messy scans, and score it against your own spreads. Pilot on one fund or strategy, not the whole book.
Record today's numbers first: analyst hours per borrower, days from package to finished spread, and errors found later.
Use the spreads already on file, or a fresh hand spread, as the answer key.
Run the extraction and score every line item exact, close or wrong, with its confidence score. Older models failed most questions on public filings, so score every line, not a sample[^36].
Recompute the covenants from the agreement's definitions. Compare with both the hand spread and the borrower's certificate[^29].
List every flag the tool raised. Then list every known issue it missed, such as a late package, a PIK toggle or an add-back over its cap.
Check where borrower data is stored and whether it trains any model. Data security was lenders' most-raised question in one vendor's 90 conversations[^52].
Price the lift in dollars: analyst hours saved each quarter times their loaded cost. Add the value of each issue caught a quarter earlier.
Run the next quarter beside today's process, then decide go or no-go with the head of portfolio management.
watchOuts: It goes wrong on extraction errors, trusting the borrower's math, stale inputs, shifting default definitions, messy data and fraud no spreadsheet shows[^51][^29][^17]. Each fix is below.
Extraction errors flow straight into covenant tests[^51][^36]. Review every low-confidence cell before the recompute runs.
The certificate is the borrower's own math[^29]. Recompute from the agreement's definitions and log every gap.
Stale model inputs led to an SEC case: Fifth Street's marks used August 2013 projections, and it paid a $1.65M penalty[^17]. Refresh inputs every quarter and record the date.
Measures of default for the same market run from about 1% to over 10%[^23][^27]. Pick your definition, write it down and keep it.

Messy data sinks AI projects: Gartner expects 60% of AI projects without AI-ready data to be abandoned through 2026[^41]. In a vendor-sponsored survey, only 8% of managers rated their data maturity high[^35].
Fraud is not a spreadsheet problem: the SEC alleges Tricolor pledged the same collateral twice[^18][^19]. Pair AI flags with lien searches and field checks.

faq.a: Checking each borrower's reported numbers against its loan covenants every quarter[^28]. Maintenance covenants, such as debt-to-EBITDA and interest coverage, are tested through a compliance certificate[^28]. It shows the borrower's own calculation, not the lender's[^29].

faq.q: Does AI covenant monitoring take the analyst out of the loop?
faq.a: No. PwC finds assistive uses such as extraction and covenant analysis are the mature ones, and people stay in credit decisions[^33]. Even a vendor selling it answers no to the same question[^53].

faq.q: Why not just put the PDFs into ChatGPT?
faq.a: Because general models make number errors: in FinanceBench, GPT-4-Turbo with retrieval failed or refused 81% of questions on public filings[^36]. That was 2023, but the lesson holds: check every number against the source. Lenders asked this 20 times in one vendor's 90 conversations[^52].

faq.q: Is our borrower data safe with AI?
faq.a: It depends on the setup: where data is stored, who can see it and whether it trains a model. Data security was the top question in one vendor's talks with 90 lenders[^52]. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework gives a checklist to put to any vendor[^42].

faq.q: Can AI write the credit memo?
faq.a: It can draft one from the spread and the flags; the analyst edits and signs it[^33]. Credit analysts ask this on Reddit, looking for exactly that first draft[^54].

faq.q: What does portfolio monitoring software cost?
faq.a: None of the platforms we checked publishes a price, so expect a quote[^46][^47][^48]. The AI underneath is cheap: document extraction lists at $10 per 1,000 pages (read 26 Nov 2026)[^43].

buyVsBuild.buy: Most funds should buy a platform and build a thin layer on top; buy outright when you have no build team and a typical process. Bought AI tools succeed about 67% of the time; internal builds about a third as often[^40]. Menlo finds 76% of enterprise AI use cases are bought[^39].
buyVsBuild.build: Build the thin layer no platform knows: each agreement's definitions, your flag rules and your memo template. Extraction and model fees are small[^43][^45]. The risk is messy data: Gartner expects 60% of AI projects without AI-ready data to be abandoned[^41].

pickElse: When you want one system for the whole credit book: look at Allvue, which says six of the top ten private debt managers use it[^46]. It publishes no price.
Portfolio data already sits with S&P: iLEVEL says 700+ managers use it, with AI-assisted data intake[^47]. It publishes no price.
Extraction and monitoring as a service: 73 Strings claims 99% accuracy with confidence scores and human review[^48]. Ask how it measured that, and on whose files.
Asset-based finance or a multi-strategy shop: a third-party comparison lists Chronograph, Cardo AI and Arcesium[^49]. We have not checked their own pages.

offer.heading: Want a second pair of eyes on your covenant monitoring? Get a free diagnostic
offer.body: Bring us your portfolio and covenant monitoring process. In 30 minutes you leave with the first step and a before-and-after measure. You get it in writing, with no sales pitch.

reviews.notes: Read as Dana, the COO. Could not tell which build to start with: recipe 1 now says builds 2 and 3 run on its spreads, so most funds start there. 'Builder' read as a hire nobody budgeted; now 'in-house or hired'. Before-and-after measure is in test step 2 (analyst hours, days to spread, errors found later). No neutral source gives a build time, so none is stated.

Tripped on spread, add-back, headroom, Required Lenders, covenant-lite and tokens. Each is now defined where it first appears: spread in table 1, add-backs and Required Lenders in the roles, covenant-lite in team-after (new Paul Weiss source), headroom in build 2, tokens as word pieces in the build 2 cost.

Asked whether one fund or strategy can pilot first and what it does to the margin. Test step 1 now pilots on one fund's 10 borrowers; the last step runs a quarter beside today's process before go or no-go. The pricing step now turns saved analyst hours into dollars at loaded cost. Build 1 shows a sourced extraction fee (about $192 a year for 60 borrowers).

Read as the head of portfolio management at a private credit fund. Missing: maturity extensions, which Fitch says now drive defaults more than PIK; added to the early-warning row and build 3's signals. Build 2 now logs each equity cure against the agreement's limit, sourced to Sidley and the Monroe amendment. Checked that the board or designee owns the mark (Rule 2a-5) and Required Lenders own waivers; own-data note says it ranks no BDC and is not investment advice.

Read as Steve. The PIK bullet read as filing trivia; it now says why it matters (filings report PIK so differently that most need extra work to compare). His worries are covered: data (watch-out on AI-ready data), security (FAQ plus NIST checklist), skills (builder in-house or hired), return (dollar pricing step), cost (unit prices dated; platforms publish none, said plainly). No Zavient fee shown, since prices are not set; offer is in writing with no sales pitch.
